summary: Specifies the MPLS Transport Profile data plane, meaning how packets are encapsulated and forwarded inside an MPLS-TP network. It is a joint IETF and ITU-T effort. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5960 defines how Multiprotocol Label Switching Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) carries packets through labelled paths, sections and pseudowires. It also sets rules for service messages and forwarding choices, including the ban on equal-cost path splitting within an MPLS-TP path.

subtitle: The rules that define how MPLS-TP labels and forwards traffic across transport paths.

tldr.problem: Packet transport networks need a defined MPLS data plane: rules for putting labels on packets and forwarding them through transport paths.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5960 adopts the MPLS and pseudowire data planes, then specifies transport-profile rules for label paths, sections, pseudowires and the Generic Associated Channel.
tldr.outcome: The RFC sets implementation requirements for the MPLS-TP data plane. It was updated by RFC 7274.

today: RFC 5960 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2010. It has been updated by RFC 7274.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
MPLS-TP is a set of MPLS functions for building and operating packet-switched transport networks. This RFC defines its data plane, the part that encapsulates packets and forwards them inside the network. It builds on the MPLS and pseudowire data planes.

The specification identifies the functions in scope and states which ones an implementation must support. It covers packets that cross a Label Switched Path (LSP), a pseudowire (PW), or a section. How packets enter or leave those transport entities is outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC explains how packets move inside MPLS-TP transport paths. It does not define how packets enter or leave those paths.

sections.title: Labels and Packet Forwarding
sections.content:
MPLS-TP uses an MPLS label stack. Routers can push a label to add a path level, pop one to remove a level, or swap one label for another. During a swap, the forwarding function treats everything after that label as opaque. A time-to-live (TTL) expiry or a pop that exposes a reserved label triggers special processing.

Internet Protocol host and router functions on MPLS-TP interfaces are optional. The RFC also requires that equal-cost multipath (ECMP) load balancing not split traffic across an MPLS-TP LSP, and that penultimate-hop popping be disabled by default. A lower server layer may balance traffic only in a way that remains transparent to MPLS-TP.
sections.plainLanguage: A router normally reads the outer label and swaps or removes it without inspecting the rest of the packet. MPLS-TP does not allow equal-cost path splitting inside an LSP, and label removal at the penultimate router is off by default.

sections.title: Paths, Sections and Pseudowires
sections.content:
An MPLS-TP LSP is an ordinary MPLS LSP unless this RFC gives it a different rule. LSP payloads can be network-layer packets or pseudowire packets. When an MPLS label stack continues into the payload, exactly one label entry in the contiguous stack has its bottom-of-stack bit set.

A section is the connectivity between adjacent label-switching routers at one level. It can be a data link or a lower-level LSP, and it provides a service to the LSP above it. A section must identify the type of payload it carries. The RFC includes single- and multi-segment pseudowire data planes but does not change their procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: A path can use lower-level links or other paths as its sections. Each section identifies the kind of packet it carries, while pseudowires keep their separately defined forwarding rules.

sections.title: Four LSP Directions and Shapes
sections.content:
The RFC includes four LSP types: point-to-point unidirectional, point-to-point associated bidirectional, point-to-point co-routed bidirectional, and point-to-multipoint unidirectional. An associated bidirectional LSP pairs two one-way paths. A co-routed pair follows the same nodes and links in both directions, so the two directions share fate.

A point-to-multipoint LSP forwards a packet over every associated egress interface. Its basic label processing is the same as a point-to-point unidirectional LSP. The RFC permits Traffic Engineered LSPs and MPLS differentiated-services modes for quality of service.
sections.plainLanguage: An LSP can carry traffic one way, pair two one-way paths, keep both directions on the same route, or send traffic to several outputs. A co-routed pair shares the same nodes and links in each direction.

sections.title: The Generic Associated Channel
sections.content:
The Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) is an auxiliary data channel associated with sections, LSPs and pseudowires. In MPLS-TP it carries control, management and operations, administration and maintenance (OAM) traffic. It must not carry client network traffic.

On a pseudowire, a first-bit pattern identifies G-ACh traffic, followed by a 32-bit Associated Channel Header that identifies its kind. On a section or LSP, the reserved Generic Associated Channel Label (GAL), value 13, marks the following payload as an Associated Channel Header. Implementations must pass enough packet context to the application that handles the message.
sections.plainLanguage: The G-ACh carries service and control messages alongside the paths. A special label or header marks these messages, and the channel is not for customer traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The MPLS data plane provides no security mechanism by itself. A client layer that needs to protect its data must provide its own security. Control and management protocols used to install label operations have security features that network operators may use.

Where a router trusts a peer, it may discard packets whose processed labels were not distributed to that peer or to a system reached through it. The RFC points to RFC 5921 and RFC 5920 for further MPLS and MPLS-TP security details.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS-TP labels do not encrypt or protect the data. A service that needs protection must add it at another layer, and operators can use security features in the protocols that install paths.

viz.caption: LSP TYPES INCLUDED IN THE MPLS-TP DATA PLANE

items.title: One-way point-to-point
items.text: A path carries packets from one endpoint to another.

items.title: Associated bidirectional
items.text: Two one-way paths form a logical pair.

items.title: Co-routed bidirectional
items.text: The paired paths follow the same nodes and links.

items.title: One-way point-to-multipoint
items.text: A packet leaves through every associated output.
